# Driving the kx CLI

`kx` manages Kimox Studio's per-project credentials and the checks that prove
they work. Every read-only command takes `--json` and prints exactly one object
to stdout.

**Always pass `--json`.** Without it you get a progress display drawn for a
person, with escape codes and box borders you would have to unpick.

## Route service work through its connector

When a task names a service, check the available skills for
`kx-<service>` before running its CLI. If the skill exists, read it: the
connector skill says which commands are safe and what their output means.
This skill says how those commands receive the project's credentials.

Treat commands shown by a connector skill as the child command of `kx exec`:

```bash
# kx-vercel says: vercel inspect <url>
kx exec -- vercel inspect <url>
```

Do not try the bare service CLI first. Its saved login or default team belongs
to the machine, not necessarily to this project. `kx exec` injects the
credential recorded for the project; from outside its checkout, add
`--project <id>`.

## Where this project's environment comes from

Two files at the root, and neither holds a value.

**`kx.env.json`** — hand-written, yours to edit. Every variable this app needs
that no connector already supplies. **Add to it the moment the code starts
reading a new variable**, or nobody else can run the project.

```json
{
  "variables": {
    "ADMIN_PASSWORD":        { "secret": true },
    "ADMIN_SESSION_SECRET":  { "generate": "hex32" },
    "PAYPAL_CLIENT_SECRET":  { "secret": true, "perEnvironment": true },
    "PAYPAL_ENV":            { "value": { "development": "sandbox", "production": "live" } }
  }
}
```

Each variable says exactly one of these:

| | For | Where the value lives |
|---|---|---|
| `secret: true` | fetched from somewhere — a dashboard, a provider | 1Password |
| `generate` | nobody chooses it: a signing key, a session secret | 1Password, made by `kx creds` when it creates the field |
| `value` | not secret and not fetched: `sandbox`, a region | the file itself |

Recipes for `generate`: `hex32`, `hex64`, `uuid`. `kx creds` (with or without
`--apply`) generates the value when it creates the field. A field that already
holds `SET_ME` is not replaced: run `kx creds --guide` and pick "Generate one".

**Making an existing variable per-environment.** Change it with `kx env add
NAME --secret --per-environment`, or by hand, then `kx sync && kx creds
--guide`. The value already in the vault is not lost and is not asked for
again: the guide asks once which environment it belongs to, puts it there, and
asks only for the other. The old field is left alone and reported as extra
until you are sure both are filled.

**Add `perEnvironment: true` when the value genuinely differs** between
development and production, and leave it off when it does not. A `value`
written as an object is already per environment and does not take it. One
field for two environments means whichever was stored last is what both get.

**`.env.op`** — generated by `kx sync`, do not edit. It maps each variable to a
`op://` reference, never a value, which is why it is committed. There is one
file per environment: `.env.op` is development, `.env.op.production` exists
only when something actually differs.

```bash
kx exec pnpm dev
kx exec --env production pnpm build
```

`op run --env-file` resolves the references as it reads the file, so the
environment is chosen by which file is read, never as the command runs.

**`kx exec` is also the form to write down.** The raw `op run` fails four ways
that never mention `.env.op` — wrong directory, before the first sync, `op` not
installed, an item the vault lacks — and `kx exec` refuses with the reason
instead, names a variable the model has grown since the last sync, and turns
the missing item into a question or, for you, into `--skip-missing` (see
"Running a command with the credentials"). A file in the project spelling the
raw form out is not a second convention: a `Fastfile` and the rest are
scaffolded once and never rewritten, so their comments are as old as whatever
generated them.

Declare one without editing the file by hand:

```bash
kx env add ADMIN_PASSWORD --secret
kx env add SESSION_SECRET --generate hex32
kx env add PAYPAL_ENV --value sandbox
kx env add STRIPE_KEY --secret --per-environment
kx env list                # what this project declares
kx env remove OLD_THING
```

**A repository that already has `.env` files.** `kx env migrate` reads
`.env`, `.env.local` and `.env.<environment>`, and writes the declaration and
the vault fields in one pass. It needs a terminal — every variable is a
decision — and it deletes nothing. What decides secret from literal, and one field
from one per environment, is under "A repository that already has `.env`
files" in `docs/connections.md`, in the kx repository.

It checks the shape before writing, so a mistyped key fails now rather than
when something does not boot.

Then, always both — the file alone changes nothing until sync rewrites
`.env.op`, and a secret with no value in the vault is a reference to nothing:

```bash
kx sync --yes --commit
kx creds --guide
```

`--commit` commits what sync wrote, as `chore: sync kx`, touching nothing
else in the working tree. With a terminal sync asks instead; without one it
prints the commands, and `--json` reports `committed` so nothing is assumed.

**A variable a connector already supplies is not yours to declare.** Vercel's
token comes from the `vercel` connector; declaring `VERCEL_TOKEN` here as well
gives one value two homes, and `op run` takes whichever was written last. Run
`kx creds --json` to see what the connectors already provide.

If a service later becomes a connector, drop the variable from `kx.env.json`
and sync: the value moves to the connector's section rather than being asked
for again.

## Never write a secret anywhere else

No `.env`, no `.env.local`, no value pasted into a file, a commit, a comment
or a message. The vault holds them and `op run` injects them at launch. If you
need one to exist, add it to `kx.env.json` and let `kx creds` put it in.

**And never read one out.** No `op read`, no `op item get`, no `export
X=$(op …)`: the value lands in your shell, your transcript and every log of
this session, which is exactly what `.env.op` exists to avoid. When `kx exec`
refuses, the refusal is the answer — see below — and working around it with
`op read` is the one thing worse than not running the command.

## The envelope

Every command answers in the same shape, success or failure:

```json
{ "ok": true,  "command": "doctor", "data": { } }
{ "ok": false, "command": "doctor", "error": { "message": "...", "detail": "..." } }
```

So parse first, branch second. A failure is still valid JSON, and `detail`
usually holds what you needed — an unknown project id comes back with the list
of real ones.

## Start here

```bash
kx doctor --json
```

Run from inside the project. It works out which project from the git remote;
add `--project <id>` from anywhere else. `kx doctor --all --json` answers
for every project at once, as `{ healthy, projects: [...] }` with the same
per-project shape, for the question "which of the studio's projects are set
up at all".

It answers the only question that matters: does this project's setup actually
work. Read `healthy` first, then `summary`, then `checks` for the detail.

```json
{
  "healthy": false,
  "summary": { "passed": 4, "failed": 1, "skipped": 2, "blocked": 0 },
  "checks": [
    { "connector": "vercel", "stage": "installed", "outcome": "passed" },
    { "connector": "vercel", "stage": "account",   "outcome": "failed",
      "detail": "Error: The specified token is not valid." }
  ]
}
```

### Reading a check

Each connector is checked in three stages, and they stop at the first failure:

- `installed` — is the CLI on this machine
- `account` — is the credential accepted at all
- `project` — does it reach **this project's** resources

The stage that failed is the diagnosis. `account` passing while `project` fails
is not a broken credential — it is a credential for the wrong account, or one
scoped to another resource. Say that, rather than suggesting a new token.

`detail` on a failure is what the service itself said. Quote it; it is more
precise than a paraphrase.

### What "healthy" means, and does not

`healthy` is true only when something was actually verified and all of it
passed. It is **not** "no failures":

All paths below are under `data`, and the first is nested a level deeper than
the other two.

- `summary.blocked` — a credential is missing or still holds the `SET_ME`
  placeholder, so the check could not run. Nothing was proved.
- `unconfirmedAccounts` — a credential was accepted, but no project-level check
  ran to confirm *which* account it opened. One service holds several of the
  studio's accounts, so this is unresolved, not fine.
- `unchecked` — connectors with no credential check written at all.

Never report a project as working on the strength of a short list. Say what was
checked and what was not.

## What is missing, and what to do

```bash
kx creds --project <id> --json
```

- `missing` — not in the 1Password item at all
- `unfilled` — present, still holding `SET_ME`. Not usable.
- `extra` — in the item, needed by nothing. Reported, never deleted.
- `moves` — a value already in the vault under a name the model no longer
  uses. `kx creds --guide` carries it across; nobody needs to find it again.
- `missingParams` — identifiers, not secrets: which Cloudflare zone, which
  Vercel project. Without them the `project` stage cannot run.
- `readFailure` — the item could not be read. When this is set, `missing`,
  `unfilled` and `extra` are empty **because nothing was compared, not because
  nothing is missing**. `required` is still right: it comes from the model.
  Reporting the empty lists as "nothing is missing" tells someone their vault
  is complete when it may hold nothing at all — say "unknown from here".
- `staleCopy` — this install is behind the shared repository, so the answer may
  describe an older model than a colleague is working from.

Also present and rarely needed: `project`, `vault`, `item` (null before the
project has one), `required` (every field the model wants, as objects rather
than names), `satisfied`, and `noteStale`.

`kx doctor --json` carries the same `missingParams`, plus `summary`,
`prerequisites`, `checks`, `credentials`, `unconfirmedAccounts`, `unchecked`,
and `fixes` — what the interactive repair would offer, so you can describe the
work before anyone starts it.

## Reading a guide

```bash
kx guide --json              # which guides exist
kx guide cloudflare --json   # the source markdown
```

Returns the markdown, not the rendered form. Use it to answer "how do I get
this credential" without sending anyone to hunt through a dashboard.

## What you cannot do

**Filling anything in is interactive and has no JSON form.** `--json` with
`--guide`, `--roll` or `--fix` refuses rather than pretending. Tell the person to run it
themselves:

```bash
kx creds --project <id> --guide   # everything not yet answered
kx creds --project <id> --fix     # only what the checks say is broken
kx creds --project <id> --interactive --roll  # choose filled credentials to replace
```

**Some commands refuse before the CLI starts.** `kx creds` and `kx add` write
to the shared `projects.json`, so the wrapper updates its own install first and
stops if that install has uncommitted changes or is behind origin. The message
is about a git repository you are not standing in — `~/.kx/kx`, not the project
— and no JSON is printed, because the CLI never ran. Report it; do not retry.

**Never ask anyone to paste a secret to you, and never read one.** Values live
in 1Password and reach a command through `op run`. Nothing kx prints contains
one, and nothing you write should.

## Which services a project uses

```bash
kx connector list              # what it has, and what exists
kx connector add neon
kx connector remove neon
```

```bash
kx connector suggest           # what the code looks like it uses
```

Suggestions with the evidence attached, and nothing is applied — it prints the
commands for you to run after checking each one. A model reading source it did
not write infers intent: right often, and confidently wrong the rest of the
time, which is fine for a list a person reads and worthless for one a program
applies.

`projects.json` is shared, so a connection is a fact about the project and not
about the branch you are on. Added on a feature branch, it applies to every
checkout of that repository — there is deliberately no "not live yet", because
a second place recording which connectors are real is a second thing to keep
true.

The consequence worth knowing: everyone else's `.env.op` is out of date until
they sync. `kx exec` says so by name rather than failing at the service.

**Fill the credential before anyone else syncs.** `op run` is all or nothing —
one reference it cannot resolve fails the whole command, so a connector added
before its value exists turns every `kx exec` for whoever syncs next into a
question: launch without these variables? A person answers it at a terminal;
you answer it with `--skip-missing`, and only for a command that does not need
them. Either way it is a question nobody should have to keep answering.

If two branches each added one, `.env.op` conflicts on merge. Do not resolve it
by hand: take either side and run `kx sync`, which regenerates it from
`projects.json`, where both already are.

Removing one deletes nothing from the vault. Its fields stop being required,
which makes them `extra` — reported, never deleted, because a credential may
be in use somewhere this file cannot see.

## Applying a sync

```bash
kx sync --json              # the plan, writes nothing
kx sync --json --yes        # applies it
```

`changes` is the count; `files.writes` and `files.stale` are what would happen.

```bash
kx sync --all --json --dry-run   # every repository: clone, plan, push nothing
kx sync --all --json             # and push kx/sync, opening a pull request each
```

Every project's repositories, each through a pull request, and never a
checkout on this machine. Needs `gh` signed in with push access and no `op`
at all, so it is one of the things you *can* run without 1Password.
`repositories[]` carries one entry each with `outcome.kind` — `opened`,
`updated`, `up-to-date`, `planned`, or `failed` with the `step` — and the
exit code is `1` when any failed. Report the URLs; do not merge them.
`files.edited` are generated files a person has since changed by hand — those
are skipped, and saying so is more useful than overwriting them.

**`--force` does not apply anything.** It means "overwrite files edited by
hand" and nothing else, so `--json --force` still returns a plan and writes
not one byte. `--yes` is what writes. Given a file in `files.edited`, you need
both.

## Running a command with the credentials

```bash
kx exec --project <id> vercel project ls
kx exec -- npm run deploy --flag-of-its-own
```

`op run --env-file=.env.op -- …` with the three failures checked first: no
`op`, no `.env.op`, or a `.env.op` the model has outgrown. Use it instead of
writing the `op run` out — the raw form fails from the wrong directory in a way
that never mentions `.env.op`, and reads as a revoked token.

Not JSON. It hands the terminal to the command and exits with its code.
Everything after a bare `--` belongs to the command, flags included.

An item the vault lacks, or a field the item lacks, is a question at a
terminal — which variables the command would run without, launch anyway? —
and a refusal without one: it prints what is missing and the variables and
exits 1 without running anything.

You have no terminal, so the answer is a flag, and it is yours to give:

```bash
kx exec --skip-missing -- koyeb whoami
```

Read the names it printed first. If the command does not need them — a
`koyeb whoami` does not need `POSTHOG_API_KEY` — re-run with
`--skip-missing`, which launches without exactly those and still names them.
If it does need them, stop: report the items and `kx creds --guide` is the
fix, and it needs a person. `--skip-missing` is never the first thing you
try, and never a habit.

A `.env.op` that names an item the project no longer uses, or lacks a
connector added since, is a different message — "does not match
projects.json" — and its fix is `kx sync --json --yes` (`kx sync --yes` at a
terminal), which rewrites a generated file and is yours to run. Then run the
same `kx exec` command again.

**Never work around `kx exec`.** Not copying the repository, not reading a
secret through `op` directly, not any other route to the same value. If it
will not launch, the options are: sync, `--skip-missing` for a variable the
command does not actually need, or stop and report — never a path around it.

`kx open --claude` is the same thing with the arguments already written down —
Claude Code, `--dangerously-skip-permissions`, this project's credentials.
`kx open --codex` is Codex with `--yolo`.
`kx open --opencode` is OpenCode with `--auto`, auto-approving permissions not
explicitly denied. All three print the command line before running it.

A person can add `--yolo` to any of them. It requires a terminal and two
confirmations, then asks for a 1Password service account token with hidden
input. The token reaches the session and its children as
`OP_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_TOKEN`, so internal `kx exec` calls authenticate without
further 1Password prompts. kx never saves it to disk. The session has all the
vault access and permissions granted to that token, including any write access.
`--yes` cannot bypass consent. Never ask for the token in chat or inspect its
value; a person supplies it through the terminal prompt.

**`--claude`, `--codex` and `--opencode` are the only launchers there are.**
No `--cursor`, no `--code`, no `--shell`. Anything else is `kx exec`.

At a terminal all three add `op run --no-masking`, because masking pipes the
child's output and a piped stdio is not a terminal. Anything whose output is
being captured is still masked.

## Exit codes

`0` when the answer is good, `1` when it is not or the command could not run.
Both still print JSON, so parse before branching on the code.

`kx verify <connector>` is the exception, and it prints no JSON at all — it is
run by doctor's stages, not by you. It exits `2` for a credential the service
accepted while something else was not ready, so that a caller does not offer
to replace a credential that was never the problem.
